Background Work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSDs) are prevalent in occupations characterised by high repetition and high force demands. Both factors not only evoke inflammatory and degenerative processes in affected musculoskeletal tissue, but also systemic responses identified by biomarkers in blood serum. Clarifying methodological aspects of biomarkers may provide insights into their predictive role in the pathway of developing WMSDs. This study will primarily assess reliability of systemic inflammatory biomarkers (CRP, TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1β) and immune cell reactivity by repeated measures in workers with constant workloads over time. Methods This observational cross-sectional study will include two groups of workers: exposed group including workers exposed to higher upper-extremity physical workloads, especially affecting the elbow/forearm/hand-area; unexposed group, including office workers exposed to lower upper-extremity physical workloads. Recruited persons are screened against eligibility criteria followed by a medical anamnesis and blood analysis. Enrolled participants undergo nine repeated measurements once every two weeks, taking blood among others. Blood analyses will determine values of systemic inflammatory biomarkers and reactivity of immune cells. The absolute test-retest reliability of biomarkers and immune cell reactivity over time is assessed by the intra-class correlation coefficient applying two-way mixed-effects models. The relative test-retest reliability is assessed by the standard error of measurement. Discussion Knowledge of and models currently describing the pathological role of systemic inflammatory biomarkers are based on highly-controlled laboratory rat experiments. This study has the strength of assessing a human population under real-life conditions. The major challenge is in participant recruitment given the intensive and complex study design. The results of this study could provide fundamentals for initiating a cohort study and be used for developing work-related stress-recovery concepts for occupations with different physical demands to identify workers who may be at risk for developing WMSDs. Introduction Musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs) are one of the most common causes of work absenteeism [ 1 ]. The majority of MSDs in the working force are judged to be work-related, meaning that workload itself is considered an important cause in a multi-causal disease process [ 2 ]. Important stress factors are high force demands, repetitive activities, and awkward body postures, which are required during a substantial part of working hours [ 3 , 4 ]. Health insurance statistics showed that in occupational groups whose activities are characterized by high force demands and repetition, there is a more than fourfold increase in the risk of, for example, tendinitis/tenosynovitis of the elbow [ 2 ]. Several workload models have tried to visualise the pathways of work-related factors eventually leading to work-related MSDs (WMSDs), all of them based on the so-called stress-strain concept by Rohmert [ 5 ]. Here, stress stands for the objective work characteristics and strain for all physiological and psychological reactions within the workers. A central principal in ergonomic work design is that the work requirements should not lead to a strain that exceeds long-term performance . Occupational health and safety enforcement authorities worldwide use standardized assessment procedures to prevent WMSDs. However, the preventive effect of such work design measures is insufficient, and the question arises as to whether previously ignored stress factors are significant for the occurrence of WMSDs [ 6 , 7 ]. In this respect, we postulate that too little attention has been paid to recovery in the work physiology and occupational medicine literature, which may actually be of particular importance for the chronicity of WMSDs, especially in the modern workplace [ 8 ]. A rat model, developed by Barr, Barbe and other colleagues [ 9 , 10 ], showed that highly repetitive voluntary movements alone but also while interacting with force demands elicit inflammatory and degenerative processes in directly affected muscle or muscles, tendons, nerves and bones and are associated with systemic responses and neurological reorganization at the levels of the spinal cord and brain. Systemic serum inflammatory indicators that inversely correlated with decreased grip strength in rat models [ 11 ] were the cytokines IL-6, TGFB1, and TNF-α and the collagen turnover proteinase MMP2. Gao, Fisher [ 11 ] concluded that serum IL-6, TGFB1, TNF-α, MMP2 but also the glycoprotein CTGF may serve as biomarkers of WMSDs, although studies in humans are needed. With regard to acute inflammatory responses in muscles and tendons caused by physical stress, best-studied biomarkers are IL-1β, TNF-α, and especially IL-6, whose concentration in serum can increase many times over shortly after exposure [ 12 ]. In addition, the acute phase protein CRP is frequently determined as routine laboratory parameter, whose concentration also responds immediately following physical exposure [ 13 ] as well as in the longer term following physical exposure [ 14 ]. Assuming that acute inflammatory processes are important for regeneration and adaptation of skeletal muscle [ 15 ], chronic inflammation leading to fibrosis may develop instead of recovery and strengthening muscle and tendon tissues, for example in cases of work-related exposures being disrupted by subsequent workloads [ 16 ]. These assumed pathway from work-related exposure to the development of WMSDs is visualised in a model presented in Fig 1 . Investigating the suggested biomarkers in a human population and clarifying open methodological aspects may provide insights into the predictive role of these biomarkers in the pathway of developing WMSDs. The current pilot study could provide fundamentals for initiating a future epidemiological cohort study. The preliminary results of the current study and (if applicable) of the future cohort study, selected biomarkers could be used in the long term to develop meaningful stress recovery concepts and related occupational health check-ups for occupations with different physical demands, thereby detecting individual workers suffering from work-related overstrain early and consequently reducing the risk of WMSDs. Aims and objectives This study is to be carried out in order to clarify open methodological aspects for the subsequent implementation of a long-term study (cohort of occupationally exposed workers). The primary objective of this pilot study is: (1) To assess the reliability of systemic biomarkers of inflammation (i.e., CRP, TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1β) and the reactivity of immune cells by repeated measures in workers with constant workloads over time . In addition, we have formulated several secondary objectives to be investigated exploratory: (2) To assess the reliability of (a) rating of perceived pain , (b) pressure pain thresholds and (c) functionally triggered pain by repeated measures in workers with constant workloads over time . (3) To assess the correlation between systemic biomarkers of inflammation and (a) rating of perceived pain , (b) pressure pain thresholds and (c) functionally triggered pain . (4) To compare the (a) level of systemic biomarkers of inflammation , (b) rating of perceived pain , (c) pressure pain thresholds and (d) functionally triggered pain between two groups of higher (exposed group) and lower workload (control group).

molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.activity_type_context: Work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSDs) caused by high repetition and high force demands, chronic inflammatory conditions, metabolic diseases, regular medication intake, inflammatory response and T cell activation induced by bacterial endotoxin and superantigen mimicry, musculoskeletal pain, and work-related physical exposure.
molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.mechanism_description: High repetition and high force demands evoke inflammatory and degenerative processes in affected musculoskeletal tissue and systemic responses. Chronic inflammation leading to fibrosis may develop instead of recovery when work-related exposures are disrupted by subsequent workloads. Chronic inflammatory conditions (e.g., rheumatism, lupus) or metabolic diseases (e.g., metabolic syndrome, hypercholesterinaemia) are known to increase inflammatory markers systemically. Regular medications (e.g., statins, ibuprofen) are known to interact with inflammatory biomarkers. LPS (lipopolysaccharide) and TStim (antibody-based mimic of a superantigen) stimulate whole blood to induce cytokine, chemokine, and growth factor production, and initiate T cell responses, aiming to identify patterns related to pathogenesis. The role of CRP as an 'inflammatory biomarker' suggests a mechanism involving inflammation, with current understanding based on highly controlled laboratory rat experiments being extended to human populations under real-life conditions.

dose_intensity_and_specificity.dose_comparison_summary: The study compares levels of systemic inflammatory biomarkers, rating of perceived pain, pressure pain thresholds, and functionally triggered pain between an 'exposed group' with higher upper-extremity physical workloads (especially affecting the elbow/forearm/hand-area, exceeding the Action Limit of the TLV for Hand Activity Level) and an 'unexposed group' of office workers exposed to lower upper-extremity physical workloads (not exceeding the TLV for HAL). Statistically significantly increased levels of CRP were reported in subjects suffering from musculoskeletal neck/shoulder pain compared to subjects not suffering from musculoskeletal pain, and a statistically significant correlation was found between CRP and neck/shoulder pain intensity.
dose_intensity_and_specificity.specificity_finding: The study protocol focuses on upper-extremity physical workloads, specifically targeting the elbow/forearm/hand-area. The physical load assessed (TLV for HAL) is specific to hands and arms. Joint mobility assessment also focuses on the forearm-region and hand-arm system. Exclusion criteria aim for specificity by focusing on musculoskeletal pain in the target area, excluding participants with other significant musculoskeletal pain, chronic inflammatory conditions, metabolic diseases, or medications known to affect inflammatory markers systemically, or acute trauma/inflammation. No explicit unique specificity finding of CRP to musculoskeletal pain versus other inflammatory conditions is detailed.

clinical_implication_and_population.target_population: Workers aged 18-67 years with continuous employment for at least one year, divided into an 'exposed group' experiencing higher physical workloads on upper extremities (elbow/forearm/hand-area, daily repetitive strain, varying degrees of musculoskeletal pain in the target area, where physical load on hands and arms exceeds the Action Limit of the TLV for Hand Activity Level) and an 'unexposed group' of office workers with lower physical workloads (not exceeding the TLV for HAL) and no musculoskeletal pain. The study aims for an equal ratio of men and women and excludes participants with acute infection, chronic inflammatory or metabolic diseases, acute trauma affecting joints or muscles, or medications known to interact with inflammatory biomarkers systemically.
clinical_implication_and_population.health_implication: The study investigates the health implications of higher physical workloads and repetitive strain on the upper extremities, including the risk of developing Work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSDs), work absenteeism, tendinitis/tenosynovitis of the elbow, and work-related overstrain. Systemic inflammatory biomarkers like CRP, TNF-, IL-6, and IL-1 are associated with the presence and intensity of musculoskeletal pain, suggesting a potential role of inflammation in WMSDs. The findings could provide fundamentals for developing work-related stress-recovery concepts and understanding potential patterns related to pathogenesis.
clinical_implication_and_population.risk_classification: Adverse risk (for WMSDs development) and diagnostic/monitoring utility (for early detection of overstrain, assessing existing pain intensity, and presence of musculoskeletal pain) related to physical workload on musculoskeletal health.

biomarker_reliability_and_future_focus.reliability_assessment: The primary objective is to assess the absolute test-retest reliability (via intra-class correlation coefficient (ICC) applying two-way mixed-effects models) and relative test-retest reliability (via standard error of measurement (SEM)) of systemic inflammatory biomarkers (CRP, TNF-, IL-6, IL-1) and immune cell reactivity over time in workers with constant workloads. Reliability of these biomarkers will also be assessed using Bland-Altman plots. The study aims to determine the temporal stability and reliability of the baseline level of selected inflammatory biomarkers over time by measuring participants before their work shifts. Reliability assessments of other measures include CMDQ (good validity, satisfactory internal consistency, medium to substantial test-retest reliability), the 11-point Numeric Rating Scale (NRS-11) (high sensitivity, good to excellent validity, excellent reliability for musculoskeletal pain), Pressure Pain Threshold (PPT) procedure (very high intra-rater reliability), and the TLV for HAL (fair to strong inter-rater reliability). It is noted as a limitation that the selected biomarkers are a subset, and temporal stability for the most suitable inflammatory biomarkers needs to be demonstrated.
recommended_alternatives: Other inflammatory biomarkers from a large pool, for which temporal stability needs to be demonstrated.
